## What this file is

This file walks you through the first session where R does real work on your project. You
will create your White Paper project folder, check your setup, move your codebook into it,
and take a first look at the example data.

Every gray box below is a **code chunk**. Click **Run Cell** at its top left corner, or click
inside the box and press **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows) or **Cmd+Enter** (Mac). Under each box this
file tells you what should appear and what to do when it does not.

Save this file in the **top folder** of your workspace, next to `README.md`, and open it from
there. Nothing in it changes the example data. Looking is all we do today.

## Step 1: Switch the course package on

`library()` switches a package on for this R session. You do this every time you open R, not
only once.

```{r}
library(v2v)
```

**What you should see:** nothing, or a short startup message. Silence means success.

**If you see `there is no package called 'v2v'`,** the course package is not installed on this
computer yet. Open `00-check-your-setup.qmd` and run its Step 3, then come back here. If
that file is not in your workspace, download it from
<https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/00-check-your-setup.qmd> and save it next to
`README.md`.

## Step 2: Check your setup

Run **AURA: Check my setup** from the Command Palette. It looks over your whole installation and
prints a checklist. Run it every time you open a project; it finds a missing piece before that
piece interrupts your work.

If you do not have the AURA Lab R Companion, run this chunk instead:

```{r}
setup()
```

**What you should see:** the Companion prints `RESULT: everything this course needs is
installed.` The chunk shows green check marks under **Required R packages**, and green checks
for the Quarto CLI and Git under **Command-line tools**.

**If something is missing,** run **AURA: Install what is missing** from the Command Palette. Without
the Companion, `setup()` prints the exact command that fixes it under **What to do
next**. Copy that command, paste it into the R console, press Enter, then run this chunk
again. If it tells you to quit R and open it again, do that: R only notices a newly installed
program when it starts.

## Step 3: Allow the project to live inside your workspace

Your workspace folder is already a project, because it came from the course template. The
tool that builds your White Paper folder notices that and stops to ask whether you really
want one project inside another. You do, so this line answers that question ahead of time.

```{r}
options(usethis.allow_nested_project = TRUE)
```

**What you should see:** nothing at all. This line only changes a setting for the current R
session; it creates no files.

## Step 4: Create your White Paper project

This one line creates the whole project folder, already named and already wired together.
The `v2v::` in front says the function comes from the course package.

The example below is named `twitch-portfolio`. **Change the name inside the quotes on the
first line to something about your own study** before you run it, using lowercase letters and
hyphens, no spaces. For example, `"podcast-ads-portfolio"`.

The lines after it are a safety check. If the folder already exists, it leaves it alone, because
building the project again would replace your files with blank ones.

```{r}
project <- "twitch-portfolio"
if (dir.exists(project)) {
  message("Already made: using the folder you have.")
} else {
  v2v::new_portfolio(project)
}
```

**What you should see:** a green check and the line `V2V White Paper scaffolded at`, followed
by the folder it made. A new folder with your project's name appears in the VS Code
**Explorer** panel on the left.

**If you see `Already made: using the folder you have.`,** you built this folder before. That
is fine: nothing was changed. Carry on to Step 5.

**If R asks "Do you want to create anyway?"** and lists numbered answers, you skipped Step 3.
Type the number next to the answer that means **yes** (the order changes every time, so read
the words), press Enter, and carry on.

## Step 5: See what the scaffold gave you

Click the small arrow next to your new folder in the **Explorer** panel to open it. You
should see these, every one already created for you:

- `index.qmd`, the abstract you write last
- `01-introduction.qmd` through `05-reflection.qmd`, one file per White Paper section
- `codebook/codebook.qmd`, the file you fill in today
- `journals/`, `data/raw/`, `data/derived/`, and `figures/`

**If the folder looks empty,** click the **Refresh Explorer** button (a circular arrow) at the
top of the Explorer panel.

## Step 6: Move your codebook into the project

This step has no code. Until now your variables lived in your planning work; from today the codebook is the document
every later step follows.

1. In the Explorer panel, open `codebook/codebook.qmd` inside your new project folder.
2. Paste in what you have so far, your draft codebook or the definitions and decision rules
   from Definitions Practice, below the line that says `title: "Codebook"` and the `---`
   under it. Every variable needs its conceptual definition, its operational definition, and
   its coding rules.
3. Under the title, add a version line and today's date, for example
   `Version 1.0, October 20, 2026`.
4. Save the file with **Ctrl+S** (Windows) or **Cmd+S** (Mac).

## Step 7: Render the codebook

Rendering turns the `.qmd` file into a page a coder can read. A codebook that renders
cleanly is a codebook another person can follow.

With `codebook/codebook.qmd` open, click the **Preview** button at the top right of the
editor (an icon of a page with a magnifying glass), or press **Ctrl+Shift+K** (Windows) or
**Cmd+Shift+K** (Mac).

**What you should see:** after a few seconds, a preview pane opens beside your file showing
your codebook as a formatted page.

**If the render fails,** look at the last red lines in the **Terminal** panel. The usual cause
is a missing or extra `---` at the top of the file. The file must begin with exactly three
lines: `---`, `title: "Codebook"`, and `---`.

## Step 8: Load the example data

The tidyverse is the set of tools we use for every data step. The next two lines fetch the
two example tables and give each one a name with `<-`, which you read as "gets."

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

chat <- v2v::twitch_chat()
streams <- v2v::twitch_streams()
```

**What you should see:** a short list of attached packages after the first line, then nothing
for the other two. `chat` and `streams` now appear in the **R** panel's list of objects.

**If you see `there is no package called 'tidyverse'`,** run `install.packages("tidyverse")`
in the R console, wait for it to finish, then run this chunk again.

The example data arrives through a function, not a file path. Loading your own source from a
file uses a different first line; every step after it is the same.

## Step 9: Look at the chat table

`glimpse()` prints every column in a table, its type, and its first few values. Before you
run it, write down three columns you expect to find in a table of chat messages.

```{r}
glimpse(chat)
```

**What you should see:** `Columns: 5`, then five lines starting with `$ id`, `$ channel`,
`$ sender`, `$ message`, and `$ date`.

**If you see `object 'chat' not found`,** Step 8 did not run. Run Step 8 again, then this one.

## Step 10: Look at the streams table

```{r}
glimpse(streams)
```

**What you should see:** `Columns: 6`, including `channel`, `title`, `game`, and `viewers`.

## Step 11: Count what channels stream

`count()` tallies how often each value appears. `sort = TRUE` puts the most common first.
The `%>%` symbol passes the table on the left into the function on the right; read it as
"and then."

```{r}
streams %>%
  count(game, sort = TRUE)
```

**What you should see:** a two-column table of game categories and counts, largest first,
ending in a line like `# ℹ 51 more rows`.

## Step 12: Confirm the corpus

Counting is how you check that the data is what you were told it is. The book says the
example corpus has fifty channels. Check it.

```{r}
n_distinct(chat$channel)
n_distinct(streams$channel)
```

**What you should see:** `[1] 50`, twice.

## When a line breaks

R returns an error message instead of a result. The usual causes are a misspelling, a package
that is not switched on, or a stray bracket. It happens to everyone and it says nothing about
your ability. Read the message before you retype anything; the wording is the diagnosis.

For errors specific to the example data, run this in the R console:

```{r}
?v2v::common_errors
```

If you are still stuck after fifteen minutes, email me the **exact** text of the error, or a
screenshot, and the step number you were on.

## You are done when

- Your project folder exists and `setup()` is all green
- `codebook/codebook.qmd` holds your codebook, with a version line and a date, and renders
- You have a `glimpse()` of both `chat` and `streams`

Bring your `glimpse()` output to the next class, where we read the data against your codebook.
